title: Names of God in the Granth
word: Names of God in the Granth
hookLine: Waheguru, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Allah, Khuda, Prabh, Akal: the Granth uses many

cards: What is God's name? It's a question a child might ask in the back of a gurdwara. Sit through a morning of reading from the Guru Granth Sahib with that question in your pocket, and the answer keeps changing.
One hymn says Hari. The next says Ram. Then Gobind, then Prabh, the Lord.

In some hymns the word is Allah, or Khuda. One book, read from one cloth-covered stand, calls on the One by name after name. A new part of the year starts here: Sikh thought, the big ideas underneath the history.

teach.b: Start with the pages. The Granth gathers hymns from the Gurus and from other saints, and they reach for the language listeners already used.
So the One is Hari and Ram and Gobind, names from the devotional songs people knew, and also Allah and Khuda, words their Muslim neighbors prayed with.
The Granth's opening line adds names of its own: Akal Murat, the Timeless Form, and the creator without fear and without hate. Why so many? Guru Arjan answers in a hymn in Raag Maru.
In paraphrase: my tongue speaks the names that describe what You have done, but True Name is Your name from before everything.

teach.h: NAMES OF DEEDS, NOT THE WHOLE ONE.
teach.b: Our names are names of deeds: the one who sustains, who protects, who made the world. Each catches one thing the One does. None catches the One.
That shapes how a name is heard. When Sikhs read Ram in the Granth, they read it as the One present in everything, not one figure from one story. The names point past themselves.
And Sikh readers draw a plain lesson from a book that sets Allah beside Hari: nobody owns the word for God, and no name has to be defended against another.

teach.h: A NAME IS A DOOR, NOT A FENCE.
teach.b: A name is a door, not a fence. One name sits at the center of Sikh daily prayer, and that's tomorrow. But the Granth keeps the crowd.

how: In gurdwaras the Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud, and listeners hear the One called by many names, among them Hari, Ram, Gobind, Prabh, Allah and Khuda, all read as names of the same One.

games.q: what does “names of god in the granth” mean?
o: secret names of God known only to the Gurus
the Granth's many names for the One, each naming a deed
a list of separate gods, one for each name in the book

games.q: names in the Granth: tap the pairs.

s: the Granth uses only one name for God
it calls on the One as Hari, Ram, Gobind, Prabh, Allah, Khuda and more.
Guru Arjan says our names for God describe what God has done
names of deeds, he says; True Name is from before.
Sikhs read Ram in the Granth as one figure from one story
they read it as the One present in everything.

games.q: you're compiling a holy book, and your hymns call God by names from two different communities. what do you do?
o: pick one name and change the rest to match.
keep every name; each points to the One.
leave out the hymns with unfamiliar names.
games.why: the Granth keeps the crowd: Hari and Allah, Gobind and Khuda, side by side in one book.

practice: List every name for God you've ever heard, from any language, any home, any song, without sorting or judging them, and see each one as a door someone walked through.
If you pray, choose one and repeat it gently; if you don't, just breathe with the list in front of you.

wordCard.voice: Names of God in the Granth. Hari, Ram, Gobind, Prabh, Allah, Khuda, Akal and more: names of what the One does, pointing past themselves to the One. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: True Name, from the opening line of the Granth.

carryVoice: Your line: many names. Each one catches something the One does, and none of them all of it. See you tomorrow.
